extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate and beginning graduate students in real and complex analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, definitions, and local foundational theorems in elementary complex analysis (complex derivative, Cauchy–Riemann equations, complex line integrals, Goursat/Cauchy theorems, power series properties) as used in a real-analysis appendix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex derivative (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: f has complex derivative f'(z0) at z0 if the limit lim_{z->z0} (f(z)-f(z0))/(z-z0) exists (as a complex number).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently: for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 s.t. 0<|z-z0|<δ implies |(f(z)-f(z0))/(z-z0) - f'(z0)|<ε. This limit notion parallels real-differentiability and will be used throughout; consider approaching along different directions in C to test existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence with real differentiability and Jacobian in M(C) (Proposition B.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: f has a complex derivative at z0 iff the corresponding real map (u,v) is differentiable at (x0,y0) with Jacobian matrix lying in M(C); in that case the Jacobian equals M(f'(z0)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a concrete linear-algebraic test: differentiability in R^2 plus Jacobian of the special form (a -b; b a) characterizes complex differentiability. Use this to translate complex differentiability questions to real partial-derivative computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy–Riemann equations (real form) (Corollary B.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f = u+iv has a complex derivative at z0=(x0,y0) then the partials satisfy u_x = v_y and u_y = -v_x at (x0,y0), and f'(z0) = u_x + i v_x = -i u_y + v_y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversely, if u and v have first partials in a neighborhood, continuous at (x0,y0), and satisfy the Cauchy–Riemann equations there, then f is complex-differentiable at z0. Use continuity of partials when invoking the converse; failure of continuity is an important anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy–Riemann equations (complex form) (Corollary B.20)
rubrics_metrics.description: In complex notation, @f/@x (z0) = i @f/@y (z0) = f'(z0); conversely, existence and continuity of these partials and the relation i @f/@y = -@f/@x imply complex differentiability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a compact way to compute f' from directional partials and to check differentiability in practice; emphasize the requirement of continuity in the converse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic/holomorphic/entire function (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: If U is a region (nonempty connected open set) in C, f:U->C is analytic (holomorphic) on U if f has a complex derivative at every point of U. If analytic on all of C, f is entire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Region means connected open set; many theorems assume region to guarantee path-connectedness (piecewise C^1 curves connect points). 'Analytic' here is the standard local differentiability notion; use 'entire' for global analyticity on C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic closure properties of analytic functions (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sums and complex linear combinations of analytic functions are analytic; products are analytic; quotients are analytic on the set where denominator ≠ 0; compositions are analytic where defined with image in domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These follow from the same product/quotient/chain rules as in real calculus. When combining functions, check denominators and domains carefully as an anti-pattern is to ignore domain restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power series define analytic functions (example & Corollary B.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a power series Σ c_n (z-z0)^n has radius of convergence R>0 then its sum defines an analytic function on |z-z0|<R; the series may be differentiated term-by-term to obtain the derivative series with same radius of convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform convergence on compact subdisks (R0<R) justifies termwise differentiation. Use this as a constructive source of analytic functions; ensure you work inside the radius of convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and existence of complex line integral (Proposition B.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a rectifiable simple arc γ and continuous complex-valued f on the image of γ, the complex line integral ∫_γ f(z) dz exists as the unique limit of Riemann-type sums (partition-based) with mesh→0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the complex analogue of real line integrals; view f as a complex-valued vector field and match with the real two-dimensional line integral. The definition guarantees uniqueness and allows subsequent estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parametric evaluation of complex line integrals (Proposition B.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If γ:[a,b]->C is a tamely behaved (piecewise C^1) simple arc and f continuous on the image, then ∫_γ f(z) dz = ∫_a^b f(γ(t)) γ'(t) dt (ordinary integral, Lebesgue/Riemann conventions as appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this formula to compute integrals; note integrand may be unbounded but is integrable in sense used here. Remarks include Schwarz-type estimates to bound |∫ f(z) dz| ≤ ∫ |f(z)| ds (arc-length).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parametrization invariance (orientation-preserving)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex line integrals are independent of the parametrization of the curve provided the reparametrization is orientation-preserving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reparametrizing a curve check orientation; reversing orientation changes sign. This invariance simplifies computations and justifies using different convenient parametrizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Path-independence <-> existence of an antiderivative (Proposition B.5 and Corollary B.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuous function f on a region U is the complex derivative of some analytic function F on U iff ∫_γ f(z) dz depends only on the endpoints of piecewise C^1 curves γ in U (equivalently ∫ over every closed piecewise C^1 curve is 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the positive case F can be constructed by choosing any path from a basepoint to z and integrating f; then F' = f. Use the closed-curve-zero test to verify existence of primitives; failure indicates no global antiderivative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate of line integrals by arc-length (Schwarz inequality remark)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a piecewise C^1 curve γ, |∫_γ f(z) dz| ≤ ∫_γ |f(z)| |dz| = ∫_γ |f(z)| ds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to bound integrals and in convergence/vanishing arguments. It's useful in proofs (e.g., estimating integrals over small rectangles to show they vanish).

rubrics_metrics.name: Goursat's Lemma (Theorem B.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic in a region containing a filled rectangle R, then the complex line integral of f over the boundary ∂R (oriented counterclockwise) equals 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goursat's proof avoids assuming continuity of f'. It uses bisection of R and a limiting argument isolating a point, together with estimates to force the integral to zero. This lemma is the key local step toward Cauchy's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goursat's Lemma with isolated exceptional points (Theorem B.80)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic in a region containing a filled rectangle R except for finitely many interior points z_j and lim_{z->z_j} (z-z_j) f(z) = 0 for each exceptional point, then ∫_{∂R} f(z) dz = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof removes small squares around exceptional points; the condition lim_{z->z_j} (z-z_j) f(z)=0 ensures integrals around small boundaries tend to zero. Use subdivision/cancellation of interior edges when handling multiple exceptional points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy Integral Theorem — local form for a disk (Theorem B.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic in an open disk D then ∫_γ f(z) dz = 0 for every piecewise C^1 closed curve γ in D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct an antiderivative F by integrating f along polygonal paths from the center; use Goursat's Lemma to show path-independence by reducing polygonal paths. Then apply path-independence to deduce vanishing of closed-curve integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral of 1/(z-a) around a circle (standard residue computation / example)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a standard circle positively oriented that contains the point a in its interior, ∮_C (1/(z-a)) dz = 2πi; if a lies outside the circle the integral is 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by introducing a smaller concentric circle around a and adding canceling line segments to form closed curves; apply Cauchy's theorem on regions not containing the singularity and compute the inner circle integral directly. This is the basic computation for simple poles and leads to residues.
